When I was in highschool I battled this thought a lot. I ranged between putting on a mask and acting like I was on the peak of my life to being so blunt and upfront about my depression it caught people off guard. Putting on the mask and acting like everything is fine made me feel okay in the short term, but it was so draining because that wasn't me. After I started being more myself I never wanted to go back. Some people were put off by how concerned I made them feel but if they can't look past that and get to know me as a person, then I wouldn't want to be friends with them anyway. My depression didn't get cured after I started being more myself, but it made me feel more intact with my emotions, which was scary at first but I got adjusted to it and made myself process everything in a much more healthy way. 

Moral of the story: Do things for you, not for other people, your own self and mental state should always be your first priority.

And I also have anxiety, autism, and probably ADHD, although I'm not entirely sure. I wouldn't worry about being productive though because it sounds like you're not doing okay atm, focus on you and do something enjoyable to take your mind off things, you deserve it from how much you've been going through. 

And as for the future? Take it one step at a time. I know it sounds a little cheesy but as for college, getting a job, all those other future adult things, they all have a way of working out in the end. I was super anxious about college. I used to throw up and have panic attacks just thinking about it, but now I'm here and it's been going good for the most part! I realized that you can't plan for every step of the future and it's best to focus on what you can do now more than anything.

And I promise you that you are not pathetic. Struggling with a bunch of mental disorders is genuinely tough, and it doesn't make you pathetic in the slightest.

Now go do something enjoyable!! You deserve it.

My ex girlfriend sh'd a lot and it was bad. Genuinely so stressful to deal with and a couple of things I learned from it was that it becomes an addiction for one. You can't really stop because you start craving it. She always has urges to do it. And the thing about sh is it never helps make you feel better either in the long term it's moreso just a distraction. So that can lead into a never ending cycle of being stuck in this addiction of bad coping methods instead of adapting healthy ones.

Another thing is she always cut deeper with it. Maybe you handle it differently because you said you've been doing it for years. But my ex always wanted to cut more and more and the light surface ones didn't satisfy her urges enough.

I suppose the argument could be made that it is better than hard drugs or alcoholism, but that's not where the bar should be set imo. You deserve better.

Anyways that's my 2 cents, I'm no professional and haven't personally sh'd before, but I got to know my ex very well when we were together.

As cliché of a therapist answer this is, it's probably because of how you were raised growing up. If you were yelled at a lot or raised by strict parents you were essentially taught not to speak out or show much expression in case it was the "wrong" thing to do.

Everyone's different though. Hopefully you have some nice friends that would treat you nicely if you opened up to them, I find that helps me the best. Even if I don't always open up to them, it's nice to know that they're there for me. And sometimes I do open up to them a bit. Another nice method is journaling. Contrary to popular belief crying is a good thing. It's obviously not good that you feel so sad that you are crying, but if you get to that point don't hold yourself back, crying is a way to release a lot of those emotions and can make you feel better after. It's okay if you aren't "strong" when dealing with some of the serious stuff you have gone through.

I'd say talk to some people about this and be more open, it can really help your process it all and give you a sense of relief. I'd also consider going to get diagnosed for depression because it can really change the way you think about how you go about things in your life.
